title: PRD (Draft) — Private Observability Minimum Pack
body:
Doc status: DRAFT (working PRD)
Last updated: 2025-02-12
DRI: Vivek Kulkarni (Product, Private)
Program manager: Talia Benson
Eng leads: Logan Wright (Telemetry), Markus Klein (Private Deployments), Sean Gallagher (SRE)

1) Summary
Redwood Private customers (VPC and on-prem) repeatedly hit “day-2 cliff” issues: they can run inference, but they lack a consistent baseline of dashboards/alerts/log pipelines to debug latency spikes, error bursts, GPU saturation, routing/fallback behavior, and control plane health. This becomes a support burden and delays go-live because every install becomes bespoke.

This PRD proposes a “Private Observability Minimum Pack” (the “min pack”): a versioned, supported bundle of dashboards + alert rules + log pipeline defaults, integrated into the Redwood Private installer / Helm charts. The pack is intended to be day-1 usable and to create a consistent definition of what Redwood considers “supported observability” for Private.

2) Problem statement (customer + internal)
Customer pain
- Operators don’t know what “good” looks like for Redwood Private: missing baseline dashboards, unclear alert thresholds, no consistent SLO framing.
- Troubleshooting is slow: support requests start from “what metrics do you have?” instead of diagnosing a known set of signals.
- Logging is unreliable in on-prem setups: drops/backpressure, SIEM forwarding failures, inconsistent formats and redaction.
- Upgrades break alerting/dashboards unexpectedly (rule parsing or provisioning issues), and customers lack runbooks.

Internal pain
- Support and Solutions spend time rebuilding the same dashboards and alert rules per customer.
- No consistent acceptance checklist for go-live (operators and Redwood disagree on what is required).
- Hard to detect “observability pack not installed / not working” issues; missing signals are discovered only after incident.

Evidence / recent inputs
- SUP-2419: “Private install lacks clear latency dashboards” (explicit request for baseline panels + thresholds)
- SUP-2427: “Log forwarding dropping events” on on-prem cluster; collector backpressure and configuration drift
- SUP-2431: “Alert rules not loading after upgrade” (promtool errors + upgrade coupling)
- Internal helpdesk: Grafana provisioning failures due to RBAC (INT-1184); request for standard checklist (INT-1190)

3) Goals / non-goals
Goals
G1. Day-1 usable observability: after install, operator can answer:
- Are requests flowing? What are RPS, latency percentiles, and errors?
- Is the runtime saturated? Is queue depth increasing? Are GPU resources bottlenecking?
- Are we in fallback / reroute modes? Are policy/routing changes correlated with errors/latency?
- Are control plane services healthy and config propagation working?
- Is the observability pipeline itself healthy (rules loaded, dashboards provisioned, logs shipped)?

G2. Standardize “supported”: define minimum signals, supported components, and acceptance criteria.

G3. Reduce support load: fewer tickets caused by missing/unclear observability; faster time-to-diagnosis when tickets occur.

Non-goals
- Not building a new observability backend (we integrate with standard components).
- Not delivering bespoke per-customer dashboards/alerts beyond baseline.
- Not delivering long-retention analytics / advanced Console features (out of scope for min pack).

4) Target users + use cases
Primary users
- Customer operators (SRE/platform ops) running Redwood Private (VPC / on-prem).
- Redwood Solutions / Pro Services during installation and go-live.
- Redwood Support during escalations.

Core use cases
U1. Go-live verification: operator runs a validation command and confirms minimum signals.
U2. Incident triage: operator uses dashboards + alerts to narrow down gateway vs runtime vs GPU vs control plane vs pipeline.
U3. Capacity debugging: identify GPU saturation, queue buildup, batching misconfiguration.
U4. Upgrade safety: validate dashboards/rules after upgrade; rollback with known good version.

5) Proposed solution
The min pack consists of:
A) Dashboards (Grafana)
- Gateway / Inference API overview: RPS, latency p50/p95/p99, 4xx/5xx, streaming disconnects
- Runtime performance: prefill vs decode latency, queue depth, batch sizes, KV cache hit rate
- GPU saturation: utilization, memory usage, throttling/clock behavior (where available), correlation to latency/errors
- Routing + fallback behavior: fallback counts/rate, route/model breakdown, region/pool selection (where relevant)
- Control plane health: policy/config store availability, auth integration health, config propagation/rollout status
- Installer / upgrade health: component readiness, pack version, rule load status, provisioning status

B) Alerts (PrometheusRule)
- SLO burn alerts (availability + latency): multi-window burn-rate style, tuned for low noise
- Critical availability / error alerts: sustained 5xx spikes, gateway error budgets
- Resource exhaustion: GPU memory high/near-OOM, CPU/memory/disk pressure for core components, node not ready
- Saturation/queueing: queue depth sustained growth, request backlog, high time-in-queue
- Pipeline health: collector drops/backlog, export failures, “missing signals” group (metrics absent / rules not loaded)

C) Log pipeline defaults
- Structured logs from gateway/runtime/control plane with consistent fields:
  - request_id, tenant (if applicable), route, model, error_code, status_code, latency_ms, tokens_in/out (where safe)
  - redaction defaults for prompts/responses (no raw prompt logging by default)
- Supported collectors/agents: Fluent Bit and Vector (initially), with recommended filters/sampling
- Supported forwarding targets: customer SIEM endpoints (syslog/HTTP), object storage, or managed log backend where allowed
- Clear knobs for air-gapped environments: offline configs, limited egress, local buffering

D) Operator documentation + runbooks
- Install guide (VPC + on-prem)
- Configuration reference (values.yaml + installer flags)
- Day-2 ops runbook (triage for missing metrics/logs; noise tuning workflow)
- Upgrade/rollback procedure

E) Validation harness + “supported signals” checklist
- Installer exposes a post-install validation command producing a pass/fail report
- Checklist maps required signals to concrete queries and expected outputs

6) Definition of “supported” (for Redwood Private)
Definition (proposal)
A Private deployment is considered “observability-supported” by Redwood when ALL of the following are true:

S1. Supported components are in use and within version constraints
- Metrics: Prometheus-compatible metrics scraping and PrometheusRule evaluation (customer-managed or bundled)
- Dashboards: Grafana (customer-managed or bundled) able to import/provision the Redwood pack
- Logs: one of the supported collectors (Fluent Bit or Vector) configured according to Redwood baseline, forwarding to a supported target

S2. Minimum signals are present with expected semantics
- Required metric names/labels exist (including stable labels like model/route where applicable)
- Cardinality constraints are respected (no unbounded label explosion)
- Required log fields present; redaction enabled by default

S3. Pack is installed and healthy
- Dashboards provisioned successfully
- Alert rules loaded and evaluated without errors
- Pipeline health checks passing (no sustained drops/backpressure)

S4. Operator can run validation and export results
- A single command produces a report that Support/Solutions can use for acceptance

What “supported” does NOT mean
- Redwood does not guarantee customer SIEM/index performance.
- Redwood does not maintain custom dashboards beyond the pack.
- Redwood does not support arbitrary third-party agent configurations; only supported collector + baseline config is in scope.

Support policy implications (important)
- If a customer deviates materially (unsupported collector, heavy customization, missing required labels), Support will triage best-effort but may require returning to baseline for full support.
- We need a clear playbook for Support: “request validation report” should be the first step.

7) Success metrics
Primary success metrics (measured over 1–2 quarters post-GA)
M1. Reduction in Private observability-related support tickets
- Target: 30–40% reduction in new tickets tagged “private-observability” / “missing dashboards/alerts” vs baseline quarter
- Note: need Support tagging hygiene; Dev Patel to confirm taxonomy

M2. Reduced time-to-diagnosis (TTD) on Private incidents/escalations
- Target: 25% reduction in median time from first response to root-cause hypothesis (Support/Solutions)
- Proxy: time from ticket creation to first actionable diagnosis message; or time to “component isolated” (gateway vs runtime vs infra)

M3. Go-live friction reduced
- Target: reduce “observability missing” as a go-live blocker to near zero for new installs using the pack
- Proxy: number of installs requiring bespoke dashboards/alerts before acceptance

Secondary metrics
- Pack adoption: % of new Private installs using min pack by default (target >80% within 6 weeks of GA)
- Alert quality: expected paging volume within policy (Sean/Allison to define); low false-positive rate in staging and first customers
- Upgrade reliability: rule parse/provisioning failures <2% across upgrades

8) Rollout plan
Phase 0 — Discovery (2 weeks)
- Compile support/solutions feedback from last 5–10 Private installs
- Finalize supported backends + versions (ADR)
- Confirm minimum signals standard (names/labels/log schema) and redaction defaults

Phase 1 — Design (2–3 weeks)
- Dashboard catalog + panel inventory (wireframes OK)
- Alert philosophy + thresholds (SLO burn windows, severity mapping)
- Packaging approach: VPC vs on-prem, customer-managed vs bundled
- Validation checklist definition: pass/fail criteria and queries

Phase 2 — Implementation (4–5 weeks)
- observability-pack repo structure, versioning, CI validation
- Grafana provisioning hooks in installer / Helm charts
- PrometheusRule bundle + promtool CI
- Log pipeline defaults + docs
- Core product instrumentation gaps (metrics labels + structured logs) with cardinality guardrails

Phase 3 — Hardening + GA (2 weeks)
- Run rules against staging load; tune thresholds and add suppressions
- Run air-gapped test plan in lab; validate offline artifacts
- Write runbooks, troubleshooting, upgrade/rollback procedures
- Support readiness: playbook, validation report workflow, escalation paths

GA criteria (exit)
- Validation harness consistently passes in reference VPC and on-prem lab
- Dashboards provision without manual steps in default path
- Alert rules load cleanly and are noise-tuned in staging
- Docs reviewed by SRE + Security + Solutions

9) Requirements (MVP)
Functional requirements
R1. Pack install is one command (installer) / one helm value toggle; deterministic version pinning.
R2. Grafana provisioning supports both:
- bundled Grafana in private install (if enabled)
- customer-managed Grafana via import/provision instructions (no manual JSON editing)
R3. PrometheusRule bundle works with customer-managed Prometheus and/or bundled Prometheus-compatible rule evaluation.
R4. Logging defaults support on-prem constraints (buffering, constrained egress, offline config artifacts).
R5. Validation report includes:
- dashboard provisioning status
- rules loaded status
- core metrics presence checks
- log pipeline health checks (at least “collector running + no sustained drops”)

Non-functional requirements
- Air-gapped: all artifacts available offline (charts + images + dashboards + rules + agent configs)
- Secure by default: no secrets in dashboards; TLS/auth guidance; least-privilege RBAC
- Low noise alerting: prioritize SLO burn alerts; avoid per-model pages by default
- Backwards compatibility: opt-in migration or safe defaults for existing customers

10) Open questions / risks
Open questions
Q1. Customer-managed vs bundled components: what’s the default stance for Private? (Need clarity on what we ship vs “bring your own.”)
Q2. Grafana auth defaults: SSO/OIDC integration expectations vs local users? What is required for “supported”?
Q3. Audit logging: what evidence do regulated customers need around dashboard/rule changes (Grafana + Prometheus config)?
Q4. Metrics cardinality: which labels are required vs optional? How do we enforce guardrails?
Q5. Log content policy: strict default is no prompt/response logging; do we provide a sanctioned opt-in debug mode?

Risks
- Alert noise causing distrust: need strong staging validation and a “do not page on this by default” stance.
- Air-gapped packaging complexity: image mirroring + chart bundling must be repeatable; Fatima to define golden path.
- Upgrade coupling: pack version must be compatible with installer and core product metrics; need a compatibility matrix.

11) Dependencies
- Core product instrumentation (metrics + structured logs) required for dashboards; coordinate with runtime/gateway owners.
- Installer integration + Helm chart support for provisioning ConfigMaps/Secrets.
- Security review for auth defaults and audit log guidance.
- Docs capacity for operator-facing install guide and runbooks.

12) Appendix: draft severity mapping (placeholder)
SEV0/P0 (page): complete outage, sustained high error rate, SLO burn fast across short+long windows
SEV1/P1 (page): severe latency increase sustained, queue buildup leading to imminent outage, pipeline failure causing blindness
SEV2 (ticket): elevated errors/latency but not rapid burn; resource pressure trending
SEV3 (info): non-urgent config drift warnings, best practice notices

Notes to self / next edits
- Add explicit “supported versions” table once ADR lands.
- Add concrete SLO definitions (availability %, latency threshold by deployment size) aligned with Sean/Allison.
- Add adoption + comms plan for existing Private customers (opt-in vs default) and release train details (Connor).
